claim: Shigella flexneri is a Gram-negative bacterial pathogen and causative agent of bacillary dysentery.
source: Shigella flexneri is a Gram-negative bacterial pathogen and causative agent of bacillary dysentery.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about S. flexneri classification and disease causation.

claim: S. flexneri is closely related to Escherichia coli but harbours a virulence plasmid that encodes a type III secretion system (T3SS) required for host cell invasion.
source: S. flexneri is closely related to Escherichia coli but harbours a virulence plasmid that encodes a type III secretion system (T3SS) required for host cell invasion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the genetic relationship between S. flexneri and E. coli and the role of the virulence plasmid.

claim: Bacillary dysentery kills more than 150,000 people worldwide per year, disproportionally affecting children under 5 years of age from low- and middle-income countries.
source: Shigella flexneri is a Gram-negative bacterium and the aetiologic agent of bacillary dysentery, an intestinal infectious disease that kills more than 150,000 people worldwide per year, disproportionally affecting children under 5 years of age from low- and middle-income countries (Global Burden of Disease Collaborative Network, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the Global Burden of Disease Collaborative Network, 2020.

claim: After the ingestion of a small number of bacteria (10–100), S. flexneri rapidly colonises the human intestinal epithelium.
source: After the ingestion of a small number of bacteria (10–100), S. flexneri rapidly colonises the human intestinal epithelium.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the infectious dose and colonization behavior of S. flexneri.

claim: S. flexneri uses a type III secretion system (T3SS) that injects bacterial effectors into the host cell to modulate key aspects of the infection process and to evade innate immune defences by the host.
source: For this, S. flexneri uses a type III secretion system (T3SS) that injects bacterial effectors into the host cell to modulate key aspects of the infection process and to evade innate immune defences by the host (Schnupf and Sansonetti, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schnupf and Sansonetti, 2019.

claim: Following uptake by host cells, S. flexneri breaks its vacuolar compartment to access the cytosol.
source: Following uptake by host cells, S. flexneri breaks its vacuolar compartment to access the cytosol (Ray et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ray et al., 2010.

claim: The virulence factor IcsA enables S. flexneri to hijack host actin and polymerise comet tails that render bacteria motile to disseminate to neighbouring cells and spread in the tissue.
source: Here, the virulence factor IcsA enables S. flexneri to hijack host actin and polymerise comet tails that render bacteria motile to disseminate to neighbouring cells and spread in the tissue (Bernardini et al., 1989; Egile et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bernardini et al., 1989 and Egile et al., 1999.

claim: Septins are highly conserved GTP-binding proteins that form heteromeric complexes (hexamers, octamers) that assemble into non-polar filaments, bundles, and rings.
source: Septins are highly conserved GTP-binding proteins that form heteromeric complexes (hexamers, octamers) that assemble into non-polar filaments, bundles, and rings (Martins et al., 2023; Soroor et al., 2021; Szuba et al., 2021; Woods and Gladfelter, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to recent literature on septin structure and assembly.

claim: Septins are involved in many physiological cellular processes (e.g. cytokinesis, cilia formation) and play key roles during infection.
source: Septins are involved in many physiological cellular processes (e.g. cytokinesis, cilia formation) and play key roles during infection (Mostowy and Cossart, 2012; Robertin and Mostowy, 2020; Spiliotis and Nakos, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple reviews on septin function.

claim: Septins form collar-like structures at the plasma membrane during bacterial invasion.
source: Septins form collar-like structures at the plasma membrane during bacterial invasion (Boddy et al., 2018; Mostowy et al., 2009; Robertin et al., 2023)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing septin structures during bacterial invasion.

claim: Septins form ring-like structures surrounding membrane protrusions in cell-to-cell bacterial spread.
source: and ring-like structures surrounding membrane protrusions in cell-to-cell bacterial spread (Mostowy et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mostowy et al., 2010.

claim: In the cytosol, septins are recruited to actin-polymerising bacteria, including S. flexneri and Mycobacterium marinum, as cage-like structures.
source: In the cytosol, septins are recruited to actin-polymerising bacteria, including S. flexneri and Mycobacterium marinum, as cage-like structures (Mostowy et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mostowy et al., 2010.

claim: In the case of S. flexneri, septins are recruited to μm-scale curvature at bacterial poles and the division site, which are enriched in the negatively charged phospholipid cardiolipin.
source: In the case of S. flexneri, septins are recruited to μm-scale curvature at bacterial poles and the division site, which are enriched in the negatively charged phospholipid cardiolipin (Krokowski et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Krokowski et al., 2018.

claim: IcsA promotes the recruitment of septins to S. flexneri.
source: Recent work has shown that IcsA promotes the recruitment of septins to S. flexneri, and that lipopolysaccharide inhibits S. flexneri-septin cage entrapment (Lobato-Márquez et al., 2021; Mostowy et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lobato-Márquez et al., 2021 and Mostowy et al., 2010.

claim: Lipopolysaccharide inhibits S. flexneri-septin cage entrapment.
source: Recent work has shown that IcsA promotes the recruitment of septins to S. flexneri, and that lipopolysaccharide inhibits S. flexneri-septin cage entrapment (Lobato-Márquez et al., 2021; Mostowy et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lobato-Márquez et al., 2021 and Mostowy et al., 2010.

claim: Septin cages prevent bacterial actin tail motility and therefore are considered as an antibacterial mechanism of host defence.
source: Septin cages prevent bacterial actin tail motility and therefore are considered as an antibacterial mechanism of host defence (Krokowski et al., 2018; Mostowy et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Krokowski et al., 2018 and Mostowy et al., 2010.

claim: A mean of 11.5% of infected cells was observed at 3 hr 40 min post infection (hpi) at multiplicity of infection (MOI) 100:1.
source: We observed a mean of 11.5% of infected cells measured by fluorescence at 3 hr 40 min post infection (hpi) at multiplicity of infection (MOI) 100:1 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Infected cells presented different burdens of bacteria following an exponential decay distribution.
source: These infected cells presented different burdens of bacteria following an exponential decay distribution (Figure 1D), reflective of the formation of infection foci (Ortega et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and a citation to Ortega et al., 2019.

claim: The median distance of bacteria to the centroid of cells was 8.74 µm.
source: For this, we measured the distance of bacteria to the centroid of cells (Figure 1E) and observed a median distance of 8.74 µm.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The median distance to the centroid of the cell significantly decreased with increasing bacterial burden.
source: The median distance to the centroid of the cell significantly decreased with increasing bacterial burden (Figure 1E), suggesting that the microenvironment of bacteria is diverse and changes as bacteria replicate intracellularly and populate the central parts of host cytosol after uptake at the host cell periphery.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: An increase of 36.9% in the cellular area of infected cells was observed.
source: To dissect the heterogeneity in host cells, we quantified an increase of 36.9% and 22.3% in the cellular and nuclear area of infected cells, respectively (Figure 1G and I), which was dependent on the infection burden (Figure 1H and J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: An increase of 22.3% in the nuclear area of infected cells was observed.
source: To dissect the heterogeneity in host cells, we quantified an increase of 36.9% and 22.3% in the cellular and nuclear area of infected cells, respectively (Figure 1G and I), which was dependent on the infection burden (Figure 1H and J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The total amount of Hoechst fluorescence in the cell nucleus increased 29.4% in infected cells.
source: In addition, the total amount of Hoechst fluorescence in the cell nucleus increased 29.4% in infected cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), indicating either an increase in nuclear volume or altered chromatin condensation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cells treated with latrunculin B decreased their cellular area (but not their nuclear area).
source: To test if this effect was due to morphological rearrangements during infection, we treated cells with latrunculin B to inhibit actin polymerisation. While cells treated with latrunculin B decreased their cellular area (but not their nuclear area) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D), the drug did not abrogate the difference in size between infected and uninfected cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Latrunculin B did not abrogate the difference in size between infected and uninfected cells.
source: While cells treated with latrunculin B decreased their cellular area (but not their nuclear area) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D), the drug did not abrogate the difference in size between infected and uninfected cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Approximately one third of uninfected cells (34.45%) were found in S-phase.
source: Approximately one third of uninfected cells (34.45%) were found in S-phase (Figure 2B and C), in agreement with S-phase lasting around one third of the cell cycle (~8 hr out of ~22 hr).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Infected cells presented a similar proportion of cells in S-phase (35.89%).
source: Infected cells presented a similar proportion of cells in S-phase (35.89%), indicating that S. flexneri infection did not block transition of cells from G1 to S at the timepoint tested.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: S. flexneri infection did not block transition of cells from G1 to S at the timepoint tested.
source: Infected cells presented a similar proportion of cells in S-phase (35.89%), indicating that S. flexneri infection did not block transition of cells from G1 to S at the timepoint tested.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that infected and uninfected cells have similar proportions in S-phase.

claim: A reduction of EdU incorporation in infected cells was observed.
source: We then assessed the amount of de novo DNA synthesis incorporated in cells in S-phase during infection. Surprisingly, we observed a reduction of EdU incorporation in infected cells (Figure 2D), which was dependent on the bacterial burden (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The reduction of EdU incorporation in infected cells was dependent on the bacterial burden.
source: Surprisingly, we observed a reduction of EdU incorporation in infected cells (Figure 2D), which was dependent on the bacterial burden (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: S. flexneri infection slows down DNA synthesis of epithelial cells.
source: These results indicate that S. flexneri infection slows down DNA synthesis of epithelial cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed reduction in EdU incorporation in infected cells.

claim: A reduction of protein translation in infected cells compared to non-infected cells was observed.
source: During infection, we observed a reduction of protein translation in infected cells compared to non-infected cells (Figure 2F and G), which was also dependent on the bacterial burden (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F and G.

claim: The reduction of protein translation in infected cells was dependent on the bacterial burden.
source: During infection, we observed a reduction of protein translation in infected cells compared to non-infected cells (Figure 2F and G), which was also dependent on the bacterial burden (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: S. flexneri induces an arrest in the host cell cycle.
source: Collectively, the cell morphological rearrangements, together with the reduction of de novo DNA and protein synthesis in infected epithelial cells, suggest that S. flexneri induces an arrest in the host cell cycle.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple observations including morphological changes and reduced DNA and protein synthesis.

claim: The first classification model achieved 96% correct identification of SEPT7 structures and 83% correct identification of clumps.
source: Performance of the model was further assessed with a confusion matrix where a separate annotated test dataset was challenged and correct number of predictions scored, showing that 96% of SEPT7 structures and 83% of clumps were correctly identified (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The second classification model achieved 80% correct prediction of manually annotated SEPT7 positive structures.
source: Correct prediction of manually annotated SEPT7 positive structures was 80% as shown in the confusion matrix (Figure 4M), with performance metrics precision, recall, and F1 score also around 0.8 (Figure 4N).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4M.

claim: The most frequent SEPT7 assembly is in the form of rings transversally surrounding the bacterial surface (66.7%).
source: We differentiated five frequent subcategories from a total of 855 cases. The first corresponds to most cases (66.7%), where SEPT7 forms rings that entrap bacteria transversally (Figure 5A and B, a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A, B, and C.

claim: SEPT7 surrounds bacteria in a tight association in 18.2% of cases.
source: We also observed two categories where SEPT7 surrounds bacteria more homogeneously either in a tight (18.2%) or loose association (6.1%) (Figure 5A and B, b–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A, B, and C.

claim: SEPT7 surrounds bacteria in a loose association in 6.1% of cases.
source: We also observed two categories where SEPT7 surrounds bacteria more homogeneously either in a tight (18.2%) or loose association (6.1%) (Figure 5A and B, b–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A, B, and C.

claim: Partial SEPT7 recruitment with only one bacterial pole being targeted occurs in 5.0% of cases.
source: Finally, we observed partial SEPT7 recruitment, with only one (5.0%) or two (4.0%) bacterial poles being targeted (Figure 5A and B, d–e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A, B, and C.

claim: Partial SEPT7 recruitment with two bacterial poles being targeted occurs in 4.0% of cases.
source: Finally, we observed partial SEPT7 recruitment, with only one (5.0%) or two (4.0%) bacterial poles being targeted (Figure 5A and B, d–e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A, B, and C.

claim: Bacteria associated with SEPT7 showed heterogeneous levels of DNA synthesis similar to SEPT7-negative bacteria.
source: During infection, bacteria associated with SEPT7 showed heterogeneous levels of DNA synthesis and protein translation similar to SEPT7-negative bacteria (Figure 6A–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-H.

claim: Bacteria associated with SEPT7 showed heterogeneous levels of protein translation similar to SEPT7-negative bacteria.
source: During infection, bacteria associated with SEPT7 showed heterogeneous levels of DNA synthesis and protein translation similar to SEPT7-negative bacteria (Figure 6A–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-H.

claim: T3SS activation was higher in bacteria found in cells with a low bacterial burden (less than 10 intracellular bacteria).
source: We observed heterogeneity in TSAR signal (Figure 7A and B). T3SS activation was higher in bacteria found in cells with a low bacterial burden (less than 10 intracellular bacteria) (Figure 7A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and C.

claim: The highest level of T3SS activation occurs in bacterial pioneers that colonise neighbouring cells.
source: This suggests the highest level of activation occurs in bacterial pioneers that colonise neighbouring cells, in agreement with previous reports (Campbell-Valois et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that T3SS activation is higher in cells with low bacterial burden, supported by a citation to Campbell-Valois et al., 2014.

claim: A significant increase in TSAR-positive bacteria in SEPT7-associated S. flexneri compared to SEPT7-negative bacteria was detected.
source: We detected a significant increase in TSAR-positive bacteria in SEPT7-associated S. flexneri compared to SEPT7-negative bacteria (Figure 7G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7G and H.

claim: S. flexneri has been shown to induce genotoxic stress.
source: Consistent with the ability of bacteria to manipulate the host cell cycle, S. flexneri has been shown to induce genotoxic stress (Bergounioux et al., 2012) and block the G2/M phase transition (Iwai et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bergounioux et al., 2012.

claim: S. flexneri has been shown to block the G2/M phase transition.
source: Consistent with the ability of bacteria to manipulate the host cell cycle, S. flexneri has been shown to induce genotoxic stress (Bergounioux et al., 2012) and block the G2/M phase transition (Iwai et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Iwai et al., 2007 and Wang et al., 2019.

claim: The OspC family of S. flexneri effectors ADP-riboxanates the host translation initiation factor 3, leading to translational arrest and the formation of stress granules.
source: A recent report has shown that the OspC family of S. flexneri effectors ADP-riboxanates the host translation initiation factor 3, leading to translational arrest and the formation of stress granules (Zhang et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2024.

claim: Cell cycle arrest would prevent maturation and shedding of infected epithelial cells, thereby promoting efficient gut colonisation.
source: In the natural S. flexneri niche of the human gut, such an arrest would prevent maturation and shedding of infected epithelial cells, thereby promoting efficient gut colonisation (Iwai et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a speculation about the biological significance of cell cycle arrest, supported by a citation to Iwai et al., 2007.

claim: Septin cage assembly around S. flexneri can start with the discrete recruitment of septins to one or two bacterial poles.
source: While previous work has shown that septin cage assembly around S. flexneri can start with the discrete recruitment of septins to one or two bacterial poles (Krokowski et al., 2018), it is not yet known if the different septin assemblies we describe here correspond to different stages or fates of the same structure or whether it marks separate biological events.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Krokowski et al., 2018.

claim: T3SS activity has been shown to be higher in motile bacteria.
source: T3SS activity has been shown to be higher in motile bacteria (Campbell-Valois et al., 2014), which reinforces the antimicrobial role of septins in counteracting actin tail motility.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Campbell-Valois et al., 2014.

claim: High-content microscopy enables the automated acquisition of thousands of microscopy images and therefore is useful to capture the heterogeneity of individual host and bacterial cells during the infection process for quantitative analysis.
source: High-content microscopy enables the automated acquisition of thousands of microscopy images and therefore is useful to capture the heterogeneity of individual host and bacterial cells during the infection process for quantitative analysis (Aylan et al., 2023; Brodin and Christophe, 2011; Deboosere et al., 2021; Dramé et al., 2023; Fisch et al., 2019; Lensen et al., 2023; Pylkkö et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to literature on high-content microscopy applications.

claim: SEPT7 is a core component of septin hexamers and octamers and is historically used to identify septin structures.
source: SEPT7 is a core component of septin hexamers and octamers and is historically used to identify septin structures (Mostowy et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SEPT7, supported by a citation to Mostowy et al., 2010.

claim: Convolutional neural networks are effective in solving classification tasks in computer vision.
source: The analysis pipeline includes two deep learning models based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs), which are effective in solving classification tasks in computer vision (Krizhevsky et al., 2012; LeCun et al., 2015; Nielsen, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CNNs, supported by citations to foundational literature.

claim: Septins can surround individual and also multiple bacteria simultaneously.
source: As septins can surround individual and also multiple bacteria simultaneously (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), we focused on individual bacteria.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The infection burden is dependent on the formation of infection foci.
source: These infected cells presented different burdens of bacteria following an exponential decay distribution (Figure 1D), reflective of the formation of infection foci (Ortega et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed distribution pattern, supported by a citation to Ortega et al., 2019.

claim: The microenvironment of bacteria is diverse and changes as bacteria replicate intracellularly and populate the central parts of host cytosol after uptake at the host cell periphery.
source: The median distance to the centroid of the cell significantly decreased with increasing bacterial burden (Figure 1E), suggesting that the microenvironment of bacteria is diverse and changes as bacteria replicate intracellularly and populate the central parts of host cytosol after uptake at the host cell periphery.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that bacterial distance to cell centroid decreases with increasing burden.

claim: The increase in Hoechst fluorescence in infected cell nuclei indicates either an increase in nuclear volume or altered chromatin condensation.
source: In addition, the total amount of Hoechst fluorescence in the cell nucleus increased 29.4% in infected cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), indicating either an increase in nuclear volume or altered chromatin condensation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed increase in Hoechst fluorescence.

claim: S-phase lasts around one third of the cell cycle (~8 hr out of ~22 hr).
source: Approximately one third of uninfected cells (34.45%) were found in S-phase (Figure 2B and C), in agreement with S-phase lasting around one third of the cell cycle (~8 hr out of ~22 hr).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the cell cycle.

claim: Aphidicolin is an S-phase blocker.
source: Consistent with this, this subpopulation of cells was fully abrogated in the presence of the S-phase blocker aphidicolin (Pedrali-Noy et al., 1980; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about aphidicolin, supported by a citation to Pedrali-Noy et al., 1980.

claim: Cycloheximide is an inhibitor of translational elongation.
source: To assess protein translation, we used a 1 hr pulse of the clickable methionine analogue AHA, which specifically labels de novo synthesized proteins as AHA incorporation is reduced after treatment with the inhibitor of translational elongation cycloheximide (Ennis and Lubin, 1964; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cycloheximide, supported by a citation to Ennis and Lubin, 1964.

claim: Nalidixic acid is an inhibitor of the bacterial DNA gyrase.
source: Only active bacteria incorporated these analogues, as the antibiotic nalidixic acid (inhibitor of the bacterial DNA gyrase; Sugino et al., 1977) and rifampicin (inhibitor of the bacterial RNA polymerase; Ezekiel and Hutchins, 1968) significantly reduced their incorporation, respectively (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is established knowledge about nalidixic acid, supported by a citation to Sugino et al., 1977.

claim: Rifampicin is an inhibitor of the bacterial RNA polymerase.
source: Only active bacteria incorporated these analogues, as the antibiotic nalidixic acid (inhibitor of the bacterial DNA gyrase; Sugino et al., 1977) and rifampicin (inhibitor of the bacterial RNA polymerase; Ezekiel and Hutchins, 1968) significantly reduced their incorporation, respectively (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is established knowledge about rifampicin, supported by a citation to Ezekiel and Hutchins, 1968.

claim: The TSAR reporter comprises a short-lived fast-maturing superfolder GFP (GFPmsf2) that is expressed in conditions where the T3SS is active.
source: To understand effector secretion at the individual bacterial level, we used S. flexneri expressing the transcription-based secretion activity reporter (TSAR) (Campbell-Valois et al., 2014). This reporter comprises a short-lived fast-maturing superfolder GFP (GFPmsf2) that is expressed in conditions where the T3SS is active, such as in broth upon addition of congo red (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B; Parsot et al., 1995) and during infection (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a description of the TSAR reporter system, supported by citations to Campbell-Valois et al., 2014 and Parsot et al., 1995.

claim: Congo red induces the expression of the T3SS in S. flexneri.
source: This reporter comprises a short-lived fast-maturing superfolder GFP (GFPmsf2) that is expressed in conditions where the T3SS is active, such as in broth upon addition of congo red (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B; Parsot et al., 1995) and during infection (Figure 7).
evidence: This is established knowledge about congo red's effect on T3SS, supported by a citation to Parsot et al., 1995 and experimental data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The data underscore the antimicrobial role of septins in associating with actively secreting bacteria.
source: These data underscore the antimicrobial role of septins in associating with actively secreting bacteria.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that SEPT7-associated bacteria have increased T3SS activity.
